passage:
The first invitation was a free Saturday workshop on confidence, and Mahima left feeling lighter. Two weeks later came a small donation for the "growth fund," then a bigger one, then talk of leaving college to work for the group full time. Each step felt like a natural follow-on from the one before.

Then the comments started to add up. Shankar, who led the sessions, told members that calls home were a distraction. The fees kept rising. Anyone who asked questions was called weak. Mahima wrote the three things in a notebook and stared at the list.

That week Mahima read accounts by people who had left similar groups and booked a talk with the college counsellor, who listened and said that feeling foolish afterwards was common and no sign of failing. The pattern began to look like something the group did, not something wrong with Mahima.

Mahima told a trusted friend, Ayesha, everything. Together they made a plan: no more one-to-one meetings with Shankar, no more sessions, a call to Mahima's parents every evening, and the parents would collect the last of the belongings. If anyone made threats, the police would be told.

qa.q: What was the first thing Mahima was invited to?
qa.a: A free Saturday workshop on confidence.

qa.q: How did the early steps into the group differ from what Mahima did after noticing the pattern?
qa.a: The workshop, donations and talk of leaving college each seemed small and pulled Mahima deeper, while noticing the warning signs, getting outside advice and planning an exit with Ayesha and family led out.

qa.q: What was Mahima probably feeling when the counsellor said that feeling foolish afterwards was common?
qa.a: Relief and less self-blame, because it showed the pattern was the group's doing and not a personal failing.

qa.q: What could Mahima do if someone from the group kept sending threatening messages?
qa.a: Mahima could keep the messages, tell Ayesha and the parents, and pass them to the police, as the plan says.

grounding: Four approaches to a high-control group: small steps that deepen commitment, noticing warning signs, seeking outside advice, and leaving with support and a plan.

passage:
The Class 5 homework for Thursday was the same for everyone: some sums, a paragraph in Hindi, a drawing and a chapter to read.

Nandini wrote the three written jobs on a slip and guessed the time beside each: ten, twenty, thirty minutes. Adding them up, she smiled. One hour. That was all.

Anirban wound the kitchen timer to twenty minutes, worked until it rang, then drank water and stretched for five. The second block felt lighter, and the last page was finished before dinner.

Meher went straight to the drawing because colouring felt nice, then copied out her spelling list. By eight o'clock only the sums were left. Her eyes were heavy, and she raced through them and got three wrong.

Pranav had planned to start after dinner. Halfway through his tea he remembered his cousin was coming at six. He took a pencil to the plan, shifted the sums ahead of dinner, and kept the chapter for once the visitors had gone. When he closed his bag, nothing was left undone.

qa.q: How many minutes was the kitchen timer wound to?
qa.a: The kitchen timer was wound to twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Meher end up with mistakes while Pranav got everything done?
qa.a: Meher did the nice parts first and left the hard sums for when she was sleepy at eight o'clock, whereas Pranav noticed the six o'clock visit and shifted the sums ahead of dinner.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling after adding up the times?
qa.a: Relief and calm, since her smile shows the work now seemed small enough to manage.

qa.q: What could Meher try tomorrow to avoid rushing?
qa.a: Meher could start with the hard sums while she is fresh and keep the drawing as a treat for later.

grounding: Four approaches to finishing homework on time: listing and estimating, short timed blocks, easy parts first, and redoing the plan when the evening changes.

passage:
When the floor shivered that April, Hafsa kept scrolling. Nothing, she thought, just a truck. By the time she looked up, her classmates were already under their desks. She had never practised what to do, and for a few long seconds her mind offered nothing at all.

Months later, in the monsoon, water crept into Uma's street after dark. Uma did not reach for the television or the cupboards. Heads first: Papa at work, Dada and Dadi in the back room, Chintu, Uma's little brother, asleep. Uma helped both grandparents up the stairs and carried Chintu up last.

Down the lane, Reena, who had finished the school first aid course, found a neighbour with a gashed forearm after a slip. Reena pressed a folded cloth hard on the cut, spoke in a low voice and asked the neighbour to stay still. The neighbour had also knocked the neck on the railing, so Reena did not shift them and waited for the adults and the ambulance.

At dawn the road to the shelter was blocked by debris. Volunteers waved Uma toward a longer lane. Uma took it, then messaged the family group with the new way and the meeting point at the school gate.

qa.q: Who did Uma carry up the stairs last?
qa.a: Uma carried Chintu, Uma's little brother, up last.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's reaction to the tremor differ from Uma's reaction to the flood?
qa.a: Hafsa kept scrolling and lost seconds because she had never practised, while Uma counted heads at once and moved the people to the upper floor first.

qa.q: What might Hafsa be feeling when she looks up and sees the class under their desks?
qa.a: Panic and confusion, since her mind offered nothing and everyone else already knew what to do.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do so she reacts faster next time?
qa.a: She could practise a drill with her family and classmates until the first action comes without thinking.

grounding: Four teen responses to disasters and accidents: people first, trained first aid, freezing at a tremor, and changing the route when it is blocked.

passage:
The teacher's request was simple: bring a model of something that stands or spins by Friday, made from what you have at home.

Ravi emptied the odd-things box onto the floor: scraps of cardboard, a few bottle caps, sticks from old ice creams, a coil of wire. He turned the pieces over in his hands until the caps looked like wheels, and a cart began to take shape.

Shreya had one sheet of thick cardboard, so she drew a windmill on paper first, with the length of each blade written beside it. Only when every piece was measured did she pick up the scissors.

Teja pressed play on a video for a lighthouse with a motor, a battery and coloured plastic tubing. He had none of them. He fumed and pushed the video away, then looked round the room and made the light from a bottle cap and wire. Slowly the model began to work.

Kavitha built a tower of cardboard tubes. It leaned and toppled. Kavitha stared at the heap and said, "The bottom is too narrow." A square frame cut from leftover card went underneath, the tubes were set inside it, and the tower stood.

qa.q: What did Ravi find in the odd-things box?
qa.a: Scraps of cardboard, a few bottle caps, sticks from old ice creams and a coil of wire.

qa.q: What did Teja's approach lack that Shreya's and Kavitha's had?
qa.a: Teja copied a video that needed parts he lacked, while Shreya planned around what she had and Kavitha redesigned after the fall; Teja's model worked only once he adapted the parts.

qa.q: What was Teja feeling when he pushed the video away?
qa.a: Frustration, because the video needed a motor, a battery and tubing that he did not have.

qa.q: What could Teja try before starting the next tutorial?
qa.a: Teja could compare the list of parts with what is at home first and plan substitutes.

grounding: Four approaches to building a model from scraps: seeing what is available, sketching first, copying without adapting, and redesigning after a collapse.

passage:
Ayesha kept a page in her notebook headed "what keeps pulling me back." Clean water appeared twice, rural schools five times. Then she asked which of those she could truly help with, and the answer was in her laptop bag: she could teach code.

Her friend Trisha had a bigger dream: education across the whole state. For months Trisha polished slides and tried logo after logo. Whenever a first step came up, it looked tiny beside the dream, and the weeks slid past with no class held.

Ayesha started small. Every Saturday she taught twenty students at a village school, free of charge, and kept notes on who came, who left early, and why.

A year later her notes told a plain story: of twenty seats, only three were held by girls. She sat with the headmaster and then with some of the mothers. Several said the Saturday afternoon slot clashed with housework, and they would feel easier with a woman teaching. Ayesha moved the class to early morning, after agreeing the timing with the mothers, and invited Jyoti, a teacher from the next village, to lead the group with her. Within two months the front row had nine girls.

qa.q: How many students did Ayesha teach on Saturdays?
qa.a: Ayesha taught twenty students at a village school.

qa.q: Why did Trisha's plan stall while Ayesha's project grew?
qa.a: Trisha stayed with the huge dream and never took a first step, whereas Ayesha began with one small class and her notes showed her what to change.

qa.q: What might Trisha be feeling when a first step looks tiny beside the dream?
qa.a: Discouragement, since any small action seems not worth doing next to such a big vision.

qa.q: What could Trisha do to get started?
qa.a: Trisha could pick one school and run a single small class soon, then build on what it teaches.

grounding: Four approaches to a purpose project: exploring values and skills, a small pilot, a vision with no first step, and changing course when the evidence shows who is missing.

passage:
Sunday was room-cleaning day in the flats on Mango Lane, and three doors opened onto three messes.

Sahil stood in the middle of his and felt his chest tighten. Too much. Then he said aloud, "Clothes first." Next came books, then toys, then the floor. With each part done, the room looked a little smaller.

Shalini scooped everything off her floor and dumped it on the bed. It made one big heap, and she could finally see what she owned. Piles grew: cupboard, shelf, and the bin bag.

Vishal heard his mother's footsteps and shoved clutter under the bed. The floor shone. On Monday morning he lay on his stomach hunting for his school shoes, and behind the bed skirt he saw the mess exactly as it had been.

The chore that kept piling up for Sahil was laundry. Every washing day the basket overflowed and the chair beside it was buried too. At last he saw that he dropped his shirts on the chair each evening, so he dragged the basket right next to it. By Wednesday the chair was bare.

qa.q: What did Shalini dump on her bed?
qa.a: Shalini dumped everything off her floor on the bed.

qa.q: Why did Vishal's tidy-up fail while Sahil's and Shalini's worked?
qa.a: Vishal only hid the clutter, so the mess stayed and his shoes went missing, whereas Sahil split the job into parts and Shalini made one pile to sort into cupboard, shelf and bin.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling as he stood in the middle of his room?
qa.a: Overwhelmed: his chest tightened and he thought the mess was too much.

qa.q: What could Vishal do next Sunday?
qa.a: Vishal could pull everything out from under the bed and sort it into piles, or do one small section at a time.

grounding: Four approaches to cleaning and chores: splitting the job, sorting from one pile, hiding the mess, and fixing the cause when a chore keeps piling up.
